MAX Layout System User Guide

Chapter 3

MAX Commands

MAX Menus

This section describes each menu item in the MAX Layout Editor. A brief description of each command is displayed in the MAX Message Area when the cursor is over the menu item.

File Menu

This menu is used create and open cells, save cells, import and export GDSII, and so on. Each menu option is described below.

    Figure 8: The File Menu 
     

New 

 Hotkey: Ctrl-n

This is used to create a new cell. A form will pop up (See Figure 9) where you can specify the path and name of the new cell.

    Figure 9: Create a New Cell Pop-up 
     

Open 

 Hotkey: Ctrl-l

Open an existing cell. A directory navigator box comes up which allows you to search for the desired cell.

Save 

 Hotkey: Ctrl-s

Save the current cell. The cell will be saved in a file called <cell_name>.max in the directory from which it was opened or created (New). If the cell is UNNAMED, a pop-up box will appear where you specify the path and cell name.

Save As 

 Hotkey: None

Save the current cell to a different name. The cell will be saved to the new name and MAX will open the new cell. The original cell will not be updated.

    Figure 10: Save As Pop-up 
     

Save Multiple 

 Hotkey: None

this command brings up a sub-menu which allows you to save multiple cells. The options are:

Save edit cell and descendents - Save the current cell (edit cell) and all cells in the hierarchy below the current cell (descendents). This will only save cells that have been modified.

Save all modified cell buffers - Save all cells currently open in MAX which have been modified.

Revert to Last Saved 

 Hotkey: None

Restore current cell to the version which was last saved. The user is prompted if this should really be done.

Copy Cell Buffer 

 Hotkey: None

Make a copy of the current cell. This will copy the existing version of the cell in memory to a new cell. The new cell must be saved in order for there to be a <cell_name>.max file on disk for the cell. This can be used if you want to save the current state of the cell you are editing into a different cell name.

Delete Cell Buffer 

 Hotkey: None

Delete the edit cell buffer (the cell you are currently editing). This will only affect the version of the cell in memory. The version on disk, the <cell_name>.max file, will still exist.

Change Path of Cell 

 Hotkey: None

Change directory where cell will be saved. The default is the location from which it was loaded.

Toggle Read Only 

 Hotkey: None

Toggle the read-only status of the current edit cell. If the cell is not read-only, this will make the cell read-only, and vice-versa.

Import File 

 Hotkey: None

This brings up the Import File pop-up shown in Figure 11 which allows you to import a file into MAX. Currently only GDSII files are supported. The GDSII Import Setup Options menu is described below.

If you click on Find, a File select box will appear. If there is an existing cell in memory of the same name as a cell in the GDSII file, it will be overwritten by the Import File command. This will not affect the version of the cell saved on disk.

The default suffices for GDSII files are .gds, .strm, or .gdsii. You may need to change the suffix in the file selector box to find the GDSII files if your suffix is something else.

    Figure 11: Import File Pop-up 
     

Clicking on GDSII Import Setup Options brings up the pop-up shown in Figure 12. Each of the options are described below:

input style - If the technology file contains multiple styles, you can select between styles. In general there will be only one input style.

scale factor - While reading in the GDSII, the layout can be scaled by the specified factor.

    Figure 12: File Import Option 
     

read only specified cells - This allows you to only read a single cell or a cell and its descendents, not the entire GDSII file. Once you click on Done, MAX will search the GDSII file for all cell names and bring up the pop-up as shown in Figure 13. You can then select the cell to load as well as specify whether to load its descendents.

    Figure 13: Cell List Pop-up 
     

set to drc clean - Do not check for DRC errors once the GDSII file has been read in. You generally want this to be selected because running MAX DRC on an entire chip or block can take quite a while. When you make edits in MAX, the DRC rules will be checked in the area near the edits.

snap to grid - Snap all coordinates in the layout to the grid specified. The default is the design grid.

convert cellname case - Convert cell names to all uppercase, all lowercase or leave them as is (default).

report rounding errors - Report rounding errors when reading in a GDSII file. Rounding errors can occur when converting from GDSII units to internal MAX units. They can also happen when snapping to a user grid, or when scaling (both GDSII input options).

report unmapped layers - Report any data found in the GDSII file on layers for which there is no definition (mapping) in the MAX technology file.

report duplicate instances - Report if duplicate instances are found at the same location. This should generally be turned off if the GDSII has lots of duplicates of cells at the exact same location (such as via cells).

All of the above options assume that there is an existing MAX technology file which matches the GDSII file. If no technology file exits, click on Create tech file from GDS file and the form will update to look like Figure 14.

    Figure 14: Import GDSII File and Create Tech File 
     

The Output Technology name is the name of the technology which will be created using the gds_input program.

Export File 

 Hotkey: None

Export the current MAX cell and its descendents to a file, currently only GDSII. If you click on Find, a File select box pop-up will appear allowing you to specify the name of the GDSII file. The default is <cell_name>.gds. If there is an existing .gds file with the same name in the directory, MAX will first have the user confirm overwriting the existing file.

    Figure 15: Export File Pop-up 
     

Clicking on GDSII Export Setup Options, brings up the pop-up as shown in Figure 16.

    Figure 16: Export GDSII Options 
     

output_style - Specify the output style for exporting GDSII. In general there will be only one output style.

Process hierarchical interactions - Turning this off will speed up the output of GDSII data. If you have used gds_input to create a technology file, then you can safely turn off the Process hierarchical interactions option and get MUCH faster (by approximately 100x) GDSII output. If you are using the mmi25 technology provided with MAX, GDSII output does much more than just write out the GDSII file. It does layer generation (nplus, pplus, and nwell) with notch and gap filling, so hierarchical interactions must be processed in this case.

Flatten gcells - Also, if you are using the mmi25 technology, you should use the Flatten gcells option to tape out the design to get proper layer generation of the nplus and pplus layers.

GDSII->ASCII 

 Hotkey: None

Converts a GDSII file into an ASCII format. This is a useful option for debugging a GDSII file. A pop-up will open where you can select a GDSII file to convert. This converted file will be placed in the same directory as the original GDSII file. The extension of the converted file is .gds_ascii.

Print 

 Hotkey: None

Using the Print command in the File menu, MAX will print the current cell to either a plotter or postscript printer using Artwork Conversion's GDSPLOT plotting software. GDSPLOT must be installed and you must have a license from Artwork Conversion to run it. GDSPLOT currently does not run from Linux.

MAX will print all layers that are currently visible in the layout with the same colors, outlines, and stipples as in MAX. Adjust colors and fill patterns before printing using the Color Editor under User Preferences in the File menu. Furthermore, turn off any layers in MAX that you do not want to plot. For example, to plot only metal layers, turn off all other layers in the MAX palette before running the Print command.

MAX will print the entire cell, including all hierarchy shown, despite what is visible on the screen -- to see what will be printed, do a Zoom to Fit Edit Cell (hotkey: v), and then move the mouse outside of the cell and Select Cell (hotkey: f). Once the top level cell is selected, select Internals, View Area (hotkey: i). Alternatively, you can specify a region of the cell to plot by clicking on Plot Specified Region Only. The default coordinates of the region are determined by the box location (See Box Area Display ) in MAX. Thus, you can either type in the desired coordinates (See Figure 18), or draw a box around the desired layout to print before running the Print command.

    Figure 17: GDSPLOT Options 
     

Note that GDSPLOT prints from a GDS file which may be slightly different than what you see on the screen. For example, depending on your technology file, the GDS file may create nplus, pplus, and nw layers, or perform other layer operations. These are the same layers that you can see by running the See Mask command in the View menu.

Before printing, MAX brings up a GDSPLOT Setup Form (See Figure 17) that lets you select the printer/plotter to print to, the size of the plot, its orientation, the font scaling, a plot title, and whether to plot directly to a plotter or to a file. Even if you plot to a file, you must choose the eventual printer/plotter and image size so GDSPLOT can create the appropriate file type.

If the Image Orientation is set to auto0, GDSPLOT will automatically select the orientation which will give you the largest plot.

    Figure 18: Specifying GDSPLOT Region 
     

If you want to print to a printer that is not in the list, you can type it in directly. You will then have to choose the appropriate plotter type and image size.

For plotters, you can either specify the plot size in terms of the common A, B, C, D, E size plots or the width and length of the plot in inches as a comma separated list. For example, if your plotter has a carriage width of 36 inches and you want a 70 inch long plot, you would specify "36,70".

The default plot command is: 

      cat %s | lpr -s -P%p

where %s gets replaced with the plot file name and %p gets replaced with the printer/plotter name when printing. After the plot is complete, the plot file is removed unless plotting to file. Why not use the simpler command: 

      lpr -P%p %s

In short, because plot files can get very large, the -s option is required to prevent the plot file from being copied to the print queue and possibly overflowing or jamming it. Unfortunately, you then must be careful to not delete the plot file until the plot is completely sent to the plotter. By using the cat command, this is partially insured.


Even with this command, you may still have to plot large plots to a file and then send them to the printer from Unix.

Setup for GDSPLOT

Setup is required to print using GDSPLOT. Also, certain simple setup procedures can make plotting or printing easier and faster for the user.

To specify default plotters with their associated plotter type and default image size, add the following lines to your .maxrc file:

The list of plotters goes into PRINT(gdsplot,plotters), for example: 

      set PRINT(gdsplot,plotters)    "hp1 laser2" 
     

The default plotter, plotter type, and plotter size are specified as follows: 

      set PRINT(gdsplot,plotter)    hp1 
      set PRINT(gdsplot,type)       "HP750C Color" 
      set PRINT(gdsplot,size)       "36,10" 
     

Note that the list of plotter types must be one of those found in the Plotter Type list in the Print form (See Figure 19).

    Figure 19: List of Plotter Types 
     

When the user selects one of the plotters from the Plotter list in the GDSPLOT Setup form, the plotter type and default image size will be automatically selected if setup as shown below: 

      set PRINT(gdsplot,type,hp1)       "HP750C Color" 
      set PRINT(gdsplot,size,hp1)       "36,10" 
       
      set PRINT(gdsplot,type,laser1)    "Postscript II BW" 
      set PRINT(gdsplot,size,laser1)    "A" 
     

In the above example, hp1 and laser1 are the names of the plotters.

You may have to experiment to find the correct plotter type for a given plotter.

User Preferences 

 Hotkey: None

This brings up a sub-menu (See Figure 20) which allows you to specify users options. Each of these options are described below.

    Figure 20: User Specified Options 
     

Wire Setup 

 Hotkey: None

Active Layer: This is the layer the wire tool will use to draw the wire. If the tool is set to auto, the wire tool will attempt to determine the correct layer by looking under the mouse when the wire is started. The Active Layer can also be set using the Active: indicator at the upper left of the MAX screen.

Default Layer: Set the first layer the wire tool will look for under the cursor if Active Layer is set to auto. This is also the layer which the wiring tool will start with if no wiring layers are under the cursor and Active Layer is set to auto.

Display spacing box: A visible spacing box will be displayed showing the current spacing of the wire being drawn, as specified in the Wiring Parameters Menu . The wire spacing can be larger than the minimum DRC spacing rule.

Snap to Wire Grid: Wire end-points and vertices will snap to the wiring grid specified in the Wiring Parameters menu. This is NOT the same as the User Grid in the Grid menu. You can specify a different wiring grid for each layer being wired in the Wiring Parameters menu. When placing a via, the via will be moved to the nearest valid intersection of the grids of the two layers being connected by the via.

Snap to Angle: Wires will be constrained to the specified angle. If the angle is set to 0, all angle wiring is allowed. The "Snap to Angle" can be 90, 45, 30, 15 or 0.

Draw Vias Using: If set to any, the code will draw vias using the first method that works: if there is a via gcell installed, that will be used; if there is a via subcell found, that will be used; as a last resort, vias will be painted using rectangles. You generally want to use the gcell option.

Via gcell name: Specify the name of gcell to use for vias, and default properties in the form: -propname value. Only used if Draw Vias Using is set to any or gcell. You can use this to specify default properties for the via, for example, to make vias symmetric by default, set it to: via -symmetric 1. You can also change this if you have created your own via gcell for use by the wiring tool.

Flylines follow mouse: If set, any flylines attached to the net being wired will follow the end of the wire. When the wire is connected, the flylines disappear.

Edit Wiring Parameters: Edit the parameters for the wiring tool. See Wire Menu for detailed information on the wire parameters.

    Figure 21: Wire Setup Pop-up 
     

Grid Setup 

 Hotkey: None

This command opens a pop-up form as in Figure 22. There is a coarse grid and a fine grid which can be defined and viewed separately. In addition, the grid can be displayed as either lines (default) or dots.

Grid Number: MAX maintains information for several different grids. This option controls which grid is the current grid. The information on the current grid is displayed in this menu. You can set up the grids differently and then switch between them rapidly using this menu, or using hotkeys. (The default hotkeys are: 1, 2, 3, 4.)

Grid visibility: Determines if visible grid is currently on or off. Can be changed by the Toggle Grid command in the View menu.

Specify Grid Set Up: If set to normal, only basic grid options are displayed in this menu. If set to detailed, all available grid options are displayed.

User Design Grid: Points and rectangles entered by the mouse will snap to this resolution.

coarse visibility: Show a coarse grid when grid is on and zoomed in far enough. The grid can be displayed as either lines or dots.

coarse grid size: The size of coarse grid, if visible.

fine visibility: Show a fine grid when grid is on and zoomed in far enough. The grid can be displayed as either lines or dots.

fine grid size: The size of fine grid, if visible.

Manufacturing Mask Grid: The minimum feature size determined by the manufacturing process; this value is set in the tech file (See Technology Source Files ).

    Figure 22: Grid Setup Pop-up 
     

If Specify Grid Set Up is set to detailed, the following additional options are displayed as shown in Figure 23.

User Design Grid X: Points and rectangles entered by the mouse will snap to this resolution in the X direction.

User Design Grid Y: Points and rectangles entered by the mouse will snap to this resolution in the Y direction.

coarse grid size X: The size of coarse grid in X direction, if visible.

coarse grid size Y: The size of coarse grid in Y direction, if visible.

coarse grid origin X: The origin of coarse grid in X direction.

coarse grid origin Y: The origin of coarse grid in Y direction.

coarse dot size: The size of grid dots if grid type is dots.

    Figure 23: Detailed Grid Setup 
     

fine grid size X: The size of coarse grid in X direction, if visible.

fine grid size Y: The size of coarse grid in Y direction, if visible.

fine grid origin X: The origin of fine grid in X direction.

fine grid origin Y: The origin of fine grid in Y direction.

fine dot size: The size of grid dots if grid type is dots.

Flatten Setup 

 Hotkey: None

This menu controls setup for the Flatten Cells command, accessible through the Misc menu. The setup menu specifies what happens to labels in a cell when you flatten it.

For each type of label (input, output, inout, global, local, comment) you can either delete that type of label, or change it into any other type of label. For example, if you specify global turns into: global then global labels in the flattened cell will be copied into the parent cell without changes. If you specify global turns into: delete, then global labels will be deleted.

You can also specify whether to flatten or preserve the label names. If they are preserved, they may conflict with other existing labels with the same name. To avoid this, you can flatten the label names, which will cause the labels to be renamed to something like: cellname.labelname where cellname is the instance name of the cell that was flattened, and labelname was the label name in the cell that was flattened.

    Figure 24: Flatten Setup Pop-up 
     

Ruler Setup 

 Hotkey: None

This brings up the Ruler Setup pop-up form which controls how the ruler snaps and whether to user absolute or relative coordinates.

    Figure 25: Ruler Setup Pop-up 
     

Ruler Snap To: If set, the ruler will snap to the nearest specified grid or edge.

Alternate Ruler Grid: The alternate grid, in microns. This is only used if Ruler Snap To is set to Alternate Grid.

Ruler Coordinates: If set to relative, the ruler is numbered starting at 0. If set to absolute, the ruler is numbered with absolute coordinates.

Ruler Font Size: The size of text displayed by the ruler. This option does not affect rulers that have already been drawn.

Clear Ruler Now: Clear all rulers.

Layout Generator Setup 

 Hotkey: None

This brings up a sub-menu which allows you to specify users options. Each of these options are described in the Layout Generator And MAX-LS chapter.

    Figure 26: Layout Generator Setup Pop-up 
     

Display Options 

 Hotkey: None

This brings up a sub-menu which allows you to specify users options. Each of these options are described below.

    Figure 27: Display Options Pop-up 
     

Show Palette: This is a toggle button to turn on or off viewing of the palette on the left side of the MAX window.

Show Cell Lists: This toggle button turns on or off the viewing of the cell lists on the right side of the MAX window. If the cell list are turned off, the Navigator Window is also turned off.

Show Navigator Window: This toggle button turns on or off the viewing of the Navigator Window on the right side of the MAX window. The cell lists will expand down into the region reserved for the Navigator Window.

Show Bottom Bar: This toggle button turns on or off the bottom bar which contains the DRC status area, the zoom bar, cursor coordinates and the box display area.

Show Scroll Bars: This toggle button turns on or off the scroll bars on the bottom and right of the edit area. The scroll bars appear only when you are zoomed in on the layout.

Dim Non-Edit Cells: Normally mask information that is not in the edit cell is dimmed. To display all mask information at the same brightness, turn this button on.

Fast Draw: As you zoom out in MAX, by default the fill patterns used for layers will change to allow MAX to redraw faster. This option can be turned off with the Fast Draw toggle button.

Show Flylines: Flylines show connections yet to be wired, as straight lines between the circuit elements to be connected. The display of flylines is controlled by this toggle button. Flylines are only visible when you are zoomed in close enough.

Show Text (labels): This button controls display of text labels. Note that even if this button is on, as you zoom out, the text of labels will disappear, and as you zoom out even further the bounding box will be reduced to `+' shaped crosses. This does not affect cell instance names or other types of textual information.

Show sub-cell comment and local Text (labels): This toggle button turns on or off the viewing of comment labels and local labels in a hierarchical design. If labels are defined as input, output, inout, or global they will always be seen if labels are turned on and the internals are shown. By default any labels which are comment labels or local labels and are in lower level cells are not visible. To make these labels visible the Show Text (labels) toggle must be turned on. Note that these Text types are always displayed in the edit-cell.

Show cell instance names: Normally subcell names and instance identifiers are displayed for subcell instances whose internals are hidden. If this button is turned off, these names will not be displayed. The subcell names will still be displayed if the subcell is selected.

Show ports: Show/hide Text ports (Text of types "input", "output" or "inout") even when sub-cell internals hidden.

Text Size Factor: This controls the zoom level at which Text labels disappear. Larger numbers make Text labels more visible when zoomed out.

General Setup 

 Hotkey: None

This brings up a sub-menu which allows you to specify users options. Each of these options are described below.

    Figure 28: General Setup Option 
     

Warp Cursor to Menu: If set, the mouse cursor will be moved automatically (warped) to somewhere within most pop-up menus.

Raise Menus on Mouse Click: If set, and a prop menu or dialog box is obscured by the main MAX window, that is, if it gets behind the main MAX window in the window stacking order and is no longer visible, then clicking the mouse anywhere in the MAX window will automatically raise and make visible the current prop menu or dialog box.

Display selected text: When you select a net, this displays all unique text on the net, which can be a very long list.

Display hierarchical paths for text: When you select a net, include hierarchical text names in the list of selected text.

Text editor: Specify the default text file editor for Display Cell Doc in View menu.

Default text file suffix: Specify the default text file suffix for Display Cell Doc in View menu.

Html browser: Specify the default HTML file browser for Display Cell Doc in View menu.

Default html file suffix: Specify the default HTML file suffix for Display Cell Doc in View menu.

Color Editor 

 Hotkey: None

This brings up the MAX color editor as shown in Figure 29. You can specify the color and fill/stipple pattern for each layer.

    Figure 29: Color Editor Pop-up 
     

If you hold down Button-1 over Edit layer at the top of the pop-up, you can select a layer to edit. The layers to edit include the background, highlight, feedback (external DRC tools) and grid layers. You can specify the color using the HSB or RGB sliders. You can also select a specific color by holding down Button-1 over Colors.

In the lower section, you can specify whether to use a solid or stipple fill for the layer. The solid fill is a transparent color and is typically used for poly and metal layers. Currently only five solid layers are allowed in MAX. If you select stipple, the you can also specify the stipple pattern. You can select one of the predefined stipples or create your own. You may also have a solid outline for a stippled layer.

If you want to revert to the original colors and fill types, click on the Revert button and the pop-up in Figure 30 will appear.

    Figure 30: Revert Colors Form 
     

If you choose Start-up Defaults, colors will be reset to what they were when you started this MAX session or after the last time you saved the colors in this session. You can choose to revert all colors to these default settings or only the color that is currently in the color/stipple editor.

If you choose System Defaults, all your personal color preference settings will be removed by deleting any color file in ~/mmi_private/max/tech for this technology, and colors will be reset to the defaults specified in the system tech file.

If you select Save in the Color Editor, you current setting for all layers will be save in your mmi_private directory in ~/mmi_private/max/tech/<tech_name> where <tech_name> is the name of the current MAX technology. The next time you bring up MAX with the technology, your color settings will be used.

hotkeys 

 Hotkey: None

This brings up a pop-up form which allows you to specify/modify the hotkeys used in MAX.

The list box contains menu entries and other commands for which you can reprogram hotkeys in MAX. The left column is a description of the menu or command, and the right column is the hotkey, or is empty if no hotkey is assigned. Click mouse Button-1 on the line for which you want to change the hotkey. Some hotkeys can not be changed (for example, Ctrl-C), and those menu items do not appear in the list.

    Figure 31: Edit Keymap Pop-up 
     

To edit the hotkey for a command, click on it with Button-1 and a pop-up form will appear as in Figure 32.

    Figure 32: Edit Key Bindings 
     

hotkey: The hotkey entry can be empty to remove this hotkey, or can be any single character (a-z, 0-9, or symbols like $ or %), a function key designator (F1 - F10 only, not F11 or F12) or a valid "keysym" name for special keys on your system, like "Left" for the left-arrow key. CASE IS IMPORTANT! "Left" is not the same as "left".

Valid keysym names vary from system to system and can be difficult to discover. Use the pop-up menu next to the hotkey: entry to get a list of possibly valid keysyms. On Sun systems, use "Next" for the page-up key, and "Prior" for the page-down key.

Sometimes the symbolic key you select (like "<") will automatically be converted to a keysym name (like "less") to make sure it will be a valid binding for the X window system.

Many keys have multiple keysym names; MAX does not detect conflicts if you use synonyms. For example, if you bind the hotkey "%" to one function and "percent" (a valid keysym synonymous with %) to another function, no error will be printed, but obviously the % hotkey will only perform one of the two functions.

Modifier: The "Alt" key modifier is pre-empted by some window managers and not passed to application programs, so it may not be usable in MAX. MAX automatically maps all "Alt" key combinations to "Meta" key combinations as well, so if you create a hotkey using the "Alt" modifier, you may be able to use the hotkey combination by pressing the "Meta" key instead of the "Alt" key. On Sun keyboards, the "Meta" key is the one with the little diamond on it.

At any time you can Revert to factory default keymap. This will revert back to the hotkey settings that came with MAX.

If you want to load the hotkey settings from a file, select Load keymap from file and a pop-up similar to Figure 33 will appear.

    Figure 33: Load Keymap File 
     

This is a list of any pre-defined keymaps on your system. These are in files named *.keymap and found on the standard MAX path: 

      ~/mmi_private/max/  
      $MMI_LOCAL/max/  
      $MMI_TOOLS/max/  
     

Your own default keymap, if any, will appear on the list, as well.

System administrators can add keymaps to this list by creating and saving a keymap in MAX, then copying their file ~/mmi_private/max/default.keymap to $MMI_LOCAL/max/new.keymap, where "new" is a descriptive name of the keymap.

If you select Done, the new hotkeys will be used in the current MAX session. The new hotkeys will appear in the help for Current Hot Keys, and will also appear in the menus.

If you check Save as default keymap for future MAX sessions, the hotkeys will also be saved in the file: ~/mmi_private/max/default.keymap and will be used in future MAX sessions as well.

Save/Revert Options 

 Hotkey: None

This saves the current settings for the grid, ruler, and so on, to the current directory in a file called <tech_name>.pref. It also adds the command to source the preferences file to the .maxrc file in the current directory. If there is no .maxrc file in the current directory, one will be created. The next time MAX is started from this directory, the preferences file will be sourced.

    Figure 34: Save Configuration Pop-up 
     

For each item, you can choose how to handle the configuration item in future MAX sessions. The options are:

ignore: This function will not save the configuration item at this time, although any previously saved information is left alone.

save: The current state of the configuration item is saved from the current MAX session for future MAX sessions.

revert_to_default: Any saved configuration info for this configuration item is deleted, so the NEXT MAX session will use start-up defaults. However, the CURRENT MAX session is unaffected (except for the palette/color editor, which reverts instantly).

Exit 

 Hotkey: Ctrl-d

Exit out of MAX. If cells have been modified and not saved, a warning pop-up will appear. If you need to save cells, select Cancel and save the cells before quitting.

Edit Menu

The Edit menu contains commands to modify geometries, Gcells, and cells.

    Figure 35: Edit Menu 
     

Undo 

 Hotkey: u

Undo last edit. There are 99 levels of undo. MAX keeps track of operations in every cell edited, so it can undo back to a previously edited cell.

Redo 

 Hotkey: Shift-u

Redo last undo. There are 99 levels of redo.

Cut to Clipboard 

 Hotkey: Alt-x

Cut the selected geometry(s) or portions of geometries, Gcell(s) and/or instance(s). They can then be pasted into the current cell or into another cell. This also works for cutting out a section of a geometry, not just entire geometries. The geometries which are cut are put into the MAX clipboard.

Copy to Clipboard 

 Hotkey: Alt-c

Copy the selected geometry(s) or portions of geometries, Gcell(s) and/or instance(s) into the MAX clipboard. The contents of the MAX clipboard can be pasted into the current cell or another cell.

Paste from Clipboard 

 Hotkey: Alt-v

Paste the geometry(s) or portions of geometries, Gcell(s) and/or instance(s) which were previously cut or copied into the MAX clipboard into the current cell. The geometry(s) are then visible and can be positioned with the mouse.

Add Wire 

 Hotkey: w

Use the wire tool to connect geometry(s). The wire tool uses the connectivity defined in the technology file. Refer to The MAX Wire Tool for detailed information on how to use the wire tool.

Edit an existing wire. First select one segment of a wire to move with Button-1 (See Figure 36) and then press down and hold the Ctrl- key and Button-2 to move the segment. Releasing Button-2 exits. The connectivity of the wire is maintained.

    Figure 36: Edit Existing Wire 
     

Add Text 

 Hotkey: t

Add a piece of text or a label to selected geometry. The easiest method is to first select a geometry on the desired layer and then select Add Text. A form comes up as shown in Figure 37 where you enter the text for the label. If the layout is only going out to GDSII, the default options are adequate.

local, global, comment - These options are used if you are going to extract a SPICE or LEF file. This information has no effect on the GDSII output file.

input, output, inout - These options are used for the MCC critical path tool. These options are also used if you are going to extract a SPICE or LEF file. This information has no effect on the GDSII output file.

point, box - The box option is used mainly if outputting LEF and is used to define the port region for a routing tool. The point option simply defines the origin of the label or text in a GDSII file. If a box is defined for a label, the origin of the text in the GDSII file will be the lower left corner of the box.

direction - This controls where the origin of the label is relative to the text.

layer - The layer option controls what GDSII layer to output the label for. It defaults to the layer under the box or point when the Add Label command was executed. To change the layer, either type in the new layer name or click with mouse Button-2 or -3 on a layer in the palette.

    Figure 37: Add Text Form 
     

Add Polygon 

 Hotkey: Shift-p

To create a non-manhattan polygon in MAX, use the Add Polygon command. (You can also create a manhattan polygon this way but it is much better to simply paint into the box with the right button.) The polygon will be drawn in the active layer. If you wish to change the active layer, you can do so by either clicking with Button-3 on a layer in the palette or the MAX layout window, or by changing the active layer at the top of the palette. If the active layer is auto, the polygon will be drawn in poly.

Use Button-1 (left mouse button) to draw the outline of the polygon by single clicking at each vertex location. MAX will fill in the polygon when it becomes a valid polygon. Polygons can only have 45 or 90 degree corners (since most processes only allow 45 or 90 degree angles), cannot have acute angles, and cannot be self-intersecting. When you are happy with the polygon, simply click with Button-2 to finish it. Otherwise, you can hit u for undo (or the right button) to remove vertices and try again.

To edit an existing polygon, select it and use Edit Cell or Object in Place in the View menu. The outline and vertices of the object will be displayed. Move the mouse close to the vertex that you wish to change and click the left mouse button. You can now add new vertices (Button-1) or remove old vertices (Button-3) just like you were adding a new polygon. Inside the edit mode, you can also change the polygon layer by clicking the middle or right button over the desired layer in the palette. While in edit mode, the hotkey m toggles between all angle and 45/90 degree mode.

MAX 4.2 is only a beta release for polygons. Interactive DRC does not work for all-angle polygons. Interactive connectivity tracing in MAX does work for polygons, but netlist extraction does not work in this release.

Add Circle 

 Hotkey: None

To create a circle or a donut in MAX, use the Add Circle command. The circle/donut will be drawn in the active layer. Click on Button-1 where you want the origin of the circle/donut to be and drag out the circle. By clicking the Button-1 (left mouse button), you will toggle between dragging the inside and outside radius of the circle and hence you can make a donut. Click the middle mouse button to finish the circle. If you want to edit the circle, simply delete it and create a new one.

    Figure 38: Circle and Donut in MAX 
     


MAX 4.2 is only a beta release for circles. Interactive DRC does not work for circles. Interactive connectivity tracing does work, but netlist extraction does not work in this release.

Array Cell 

 Hotkey: None

First select a the Gcell, group (See Group Objects ) or instance you want to array. When you select Array Cell, the pop-up in Figure 39 will appear. You can specify how many columns and rows to array. By default, the cells will be abutted using the bounding box of all layers in the cell. Alternately, you can select a specific layer to use for abutment. If you want additional spacing between cells, use the relative dx and relative dy options.

    Figure 39: Array Cell Pop-up 
     

Edit Text 

 Hotkey: Shift-t

Edit the selected text. You first select the text you want to edit and then select Edit Text. The form in Figure 37 will come up and allow you to make any changes. Mouse Button-1 repositions either the point or the box. If the label is a point, click once with Button-1 at the new location. If the label is a box, hold down and drag the new location and size of the box.

Edit Multiple Text 

 Hotkey: None

This command can be used to automate the naming of busses. First, put a label on each bit of the bus. It does not matter what the label is. The easiest way to do this is to duplicate the label. Once there are labels on each bit of the bus, draw a box around the labels for the bus (be sure that no other labels are selected). Then select Edit Multiple Text and the form in Figure 40 will appear.

To change the names of the labels, select the Change Label Names toggle button. In the example in Figure 40 the labels will be named my_bus<0>, my_bus<1>, and so on. Bit 0 is on the bottom and they increment going up (n for north).

The direction is either n, s, e, or w. This controls where the bus naming starts and therefore which direction the naming increments. A direction of "n" means that the naming starts at the bottom label and increments north (up).

To change the kind of all selected labels, select the Change Label Kind toggle. Kind can be input, output, inout, global, local, or comment. If Change Label Kind is toggled off, the type of label is taken from each selected label. The label's layer and position can also be changed in this form.

    Figure 40: Edit Multiple Text Form 
     

Edit Rectangle Edge 

 Hotkey: a

Edit an edge of a geometry. This allows you to stretch the edge of a single geometry. First, select Edit Rectangle Edge. As you move over an edge of a rectangle, you will see a white bar (See Figure 41). Once you have the desired edge highlighted, hold down Button-1 and drag the edge to the desired location.

    Figure 41: Edit Rectangle Edge 
     

Edit Flylines 

 Hotkey: Ctrl-f

This allows the user to add flylines to the layout cell. If you have used the layout generator, flylines are automatically added to the layout. If you complete a connection, the flyline disappears. If you then break that connection, currently the flyline will not reappear. You would use the Edit Flylines command to manually re-insert the flyline.

Select Edit Flylines and then click with Button-1 on the two geometries between which the flyline is to be drawn.

Edit Properties 

 Hotkey: p

View and edit the properties of an object. For Gcells, this would bring up the Gcells properties form as shown in Figure 42. Each of the options are described below.

    Figure 42: Edit FET Gcell 
     

type: Specifies the type of fet that will be produced. The types of fets this gcell can create are specified by the device statements in the technology file.

width: Specifies the width of the fet. This fet generator has a minimum fet width of one contact width.

length: Specifies the length of the fet.

fingers: Specifies the number of fet gates. If fingers is >1, then a stacked fet will be created.

contacts: Contacts can be specified to be right (on the right side of the fet only), left (on the left side of the fet only), both (on both the right and left sides of the fet), or all (on all source/drain regions of the fet, only different from both if the fet has multiple fingers).

    Figure 43: FET Gcell Properties 
     

left_contacts: With this option you can specify specific locations for each contact. Figure 43 shows the left_contacts in positions 1, 3, 1nd 5 starting from the bottom.

right_contacts: With this option you can specify specific locations for each contact. Figure 43 shows using the "+" and "-" operators to control where not to put contacts. "+2" removes the bottom two contacts. "-1" removes the top one contact.

contact_style: If the technology file supports metal enclose contact rule that is assymetric, ie, that allows the enclosure to be smaller in one direction than the other, this option specifies how the metal over the contact will be drawn. If normal, the metal enclosure of contact will be the same on all sides. If minimum_x_overlap or minimum_y_overlap, the contact will be drawn to minimize the metal in the direction corresponding to the x or y direction of the fet in standard orientation.

If you have a rectangle selected, Edit Properties brings up a form (See Figure 44) where the lower-left corner, width, and height of the rectangle can be changed. This is also how you can change the layer of a rectangle.

    Figure 44: Edit Rectangle Properties 
     

If the selected object is an instance, the Cell Properties form as shown in Figure 45 will appear. This is where you can change the instance name (Cell Id) for an instance. This form also tells you which directory it is getting the parent cell from and any flags on the cell (available, readonly, modified).

Currently, you can edit object properties only for Gcells, rectangles and instances.

    Figure 45: Cell Properties Form 
     

Delete 

 Hotkey: q or <Del>

Delete the selected geometry(s) or portions of geometries, Gcell(s) and/or instance(s). This differs from Cut in that the geometries and/or cells are not put into a buffer, so they can not be pasted.

If you want to delete a portion of a rectangle, draw a box (with Button-1) which includes the area to cut. Then either use the Delete command or go to a area in the layout window which does not have paint and click with Button-3. Note: This only works for rectangles, not for polygons or circles.

Duplicate 

 Hotkey: d

Duplicate the selected geometry(s), Gcells and/or instances. Once the geometry(s) have been duplicated, you use Button-2 (middle mouse button) to move and place the geometry(s).

 Hotkey: None

This brings up a sub-menu which allows you to flip or rotate the selected geometries.

Flip Upside-Down 

 Hotkey: y

Flip the selected geometry(s) vertically or upside down. This flips around the center of the bounding box of the selected items.

Flip Sideways 

 Hotkey: x

Flip the selected geometry(s) horizontally or sideways. This flips around the center of the bounding box of the selected items.

 Hotkey: r

Move 

 Hotkey: Shift-<arrow keys>

Move the selected geometry(s) or portions selected by the box, Gcell(s) and/or instance(s). If an entire geometry is selected, the entire geometry will be moved. If only a portion of a geometry(s) is selected (surrounded by the box) the geometry(s) will be cut or separated into two pieces when the selection is moved (See Figure 46).

The Shift-arrow keys allow moves of one grid point at a time. Using just the middle mouse button (Button-2) allows free movement. Shift-Button-2 locks the movement to either the X or Y direction.

    Figure 46: Move Down Command Example 
     

If you select the Move sub-menu from the Edit menu, you will notice that you can also move by 10x the grid. You can specify hotkeys for these options in the hotkeys options pop-up.

    Figure 47: Move Menu 
     

If you select Move To, the pop-up in Figure 48 appears for an absolute move.You specify coordinates to move to and the reference point for the move. If center is selected for the reference point, the center of the selection is rounded to the nearest manufacturing grid.

    Figure 48: Move To Form 
     

If you select a relative move for Move To, the form will update as in Figure 49. You then specify how far to move in the X and Y direction.

    Figure 49: Move To - Relative Form 
     

If you select Move To Point from the Move sub-menu, you will be prompted to enter with mouse Button-1 the from and to locations.

The Move To Box option moves the lower left corner of the selected objects to the lower left corner of the box.

The Move Edit Cell Origin option moves the origin to the specified location. The easiest way to specify the location for the origin is to use the box to get the coordinates as shown in Figure 50. You first set Display on status bar, box to origin+size by clicking with Button-1 on the Box Area Display in the lower right corner of the MAX window.

In this example, if you want the new origin of the cell to be the lower left corner of the cell, you select the top level cell by moving the mouse outside of the cell and typing the hotkey f (Select Cell from the Misc menu).  Hotkey: <arrow keys>

Stretch the edges of the geometry(s) selected. If an entire geometry is selected, this command will simply move the geometry. See Figure 52 for an example of the stretch down command. In this case, the horizontal edges enclosed within the box are stretched down.

The arrow keys allow stretches of one grid point at a time. Holding down the Ctrl key and the middle mouse button (Button-2) allows free movement for stretching while locking in either the X or Y direction.

    Figure 51: Stretch Menu 
     

If you select the Stretch sub-menu from the Edit menu, you will notice that you can also stretch by 10x the grid. You can specify hotkeys for these options in the hotkeys options pop-up.

    Figure 52: Stretch Down Command Example 
     

If a Gcell is selected, Stretch Selected Gcell does the same thing as the Edit Cell or Object in Place command for Gcells. See Stretching Gcells for more information on stretching Gcells.

Fill 

 Hotkey: Ctrl-<arrow keys>

Extend the geometry(s) to the edge of the box in the direction specified. In the example in Figure 53, the fill down option is selected. The geometries selected by the box will be extended/filled down to the bottom of the box. What layer is extended and the width of the layer is determined by the top edge of the box.

    Figure 53: Extend Down Command Example 1 
     

In the example in Figure 54, the fill down option is selected again, but this time notice the top edge of the box intersects the wider via region. This time the width of the Metal1 extended to the bottom of the box is the width of the via region.

Align Objects 

 Hotkey: Ctrl-a

Align selected objects: You can only align gcells, cells, and text.

    Figure 55: Align Objects Form 
     

If you select left, right, tops or bottoms, the specified side of each object is aligned with the specified side of the current box. Usually the box is over the last object selected, so other objects are aligned with the last object selected. Alternatively, you can place a box with the b command, to which the objects will be aligned. If you select Individually to Grid, all selected objects are nudged until their lower left corners are aligned on the current User Grid, as specified in the Grid menu.

Align cells using: If you select cell bounding box, the cells are aligned using the edges of their bounding boxes. If you select cell origin the cells are aligned such that the cell origin inside the cell is aligned in the current cell.

"Align center" is not allowed because this could create off grid geometries.

 Hotkey: e

Push into the selected instance. If an instance is visible, it can be selected and pushed into for editing no matter how far down in the hierarchy it exists. If a Gcell is selected, the Push command brings up the Edit Properties form for the Gcell.

 Hotkey: Ctrl-e

Pop back to the previous edit cell or the root (top level) cell.

 Hotkey: Shift-e

Edit the selected cell or object in place. For cells, this command works the same as the Push into Cell command except that the non-edit cells are visible. The paint in the cell which is in edit mode appears brighter. The paint in the non-edit cells is dimmed by default. Dimming the non-edit cell paint can be turned off with the Dim Non-Edit Cells (see page 41) toggle button in the Display Options. The Pop out of command can be used to pop back up the hierarchy.

If a Gcell has been selected, this command puts you into the Gcell edit mode which allows you to stretch the Gcell. See Stretching Gcells for more information on stretching Gcells.

Dimming the non-edit cell paint can be turned off with the Dim Non-Edit Cells (see page 41) toggle button. The Pop out of command can be used to pop back up the hierarchy.

 Hotkey: None

Internals, View Area 

 Hotkey: i

Show all internals for the instance(s) under the box all the way down to the bottom level of hierarchy. The easiest way to use this command is to use the Select Cell command (hotkey: f) to select an instance of a cell (this also draws the box around the instance) and then select Internals, Show Area. This option will show (make visible) all levels of hierarchy.

If you want to show internals of the entire edit cell, move the mouse outside of the cell area and use the Select Cell command. This will select the topmost cell in the window and draw the box around it. Now when you show internals, all internals at all levels of hierarchy are visible.

Internals, Hide Area 

 Hotkey: h

This is the opposite of Internals, Show Area. The instances under the box will be "turned off" or hidden.

Internals, View Cell 

 Hotkey: Shift-i

Show internals of selected instance(s) one hierarchy level down. The easiest way to use this command is to use the Select Cell command (hotkey: f) to select an instance of a cell. Then use the Internals, Show command. One level of hierarchy down from the selected instance is now visible. You can now select one of the visible instances and show the internals of that cell.

MAX remembers which instances were turned on, so if you use the Internals, Hide Cell command to hide the internals, when you do another Internals, Show Cell of the same instance MAX remembers the state of the sub-instances (whether they were visible or not).

Internals, Hide Cell 

 Hotkey: Shift-h

This is the opposite of the Internals, Show Cell command. Hide internals one hierarchy level down from the instance(s) selected.

Tool Menu

The Tool menu contains links to additional development tools from MMT, such as the MegaCell Compiler and the Layout Generator. The MegaCell Compiler (MCC) is described in more detail in the Micro Magic Tools MCC MegaCell Compiler Manual.

SUE Cross Probe Init. 

 Hotkey: None

When you select this command, the pop-up shown in Figure 59 will appear. It lists all the SUE sessions currently running on your computer. If you already have the corresponding cell loaded in SUE, select that copy of SUE. Otherwise, you can start a new copy of SUE.

The SUE executable for new sue specifies which command to execute to run SUE. You may have a shell wrapper script that gets executed at your site. If you have multiple monitors on your computer, X display for new sue controls the initial SUE startup monitor.

SUE needs to find a matching schematic in your current directory, <cell_name>.sue. If your SUE schematic is in a different directory, it is easiest to first start up SUE with the schematic loaded. Refer to Search Paths in MAX for more details on how to crossprobe if cells have different names or are in different directories.

    Figure 59: Cross Probe Popup 
     

This command will first load the cell. If there is a matching schematic and sim netlist of the current cell in SUE, this command will run Gemini LVS to compare the layout to the schematic. Gemini LVS actually compares the .sim netlist files between layout and schematic, therefore a sim netlist must first be generated from the schematic before SUE Cross Probe Init is run. The nets that match between MAX and SUE will be highlighted in MAX with the highlight layer (See Edit Layers ), and highlighted in SUE in blue.

If SUE is already running, it must be able to find the cell in the loaded libraries.

SUE Cross Probe Net 

 Hotkey: k

First select a net in MAX and then select SUE Cross Probe Net. If there is a match for the selected net in SUE, that net will be highlighted in SUE.

SUE LVS 

 Hotkey: None

Run GEMINI LVS for the current cell. This command will look for the .sim netlist from the SUE schematic named <cell_name>.sue. It will extract a .sim netlist from MAX and call the netlist <cell_name>_lay.sim. Finally, it will run Gemini and compare the two netlists.

Layout Generator 

 Hotkey: None

The layout generator converts a schematic to a layout containing fets with flylines to indicate connectivity. See Introduction To The MAX Layout Generator for detailed information.

Calibre DRC 

 Hotkey: None

This will run Mentor Graphics' Calibre DRC program on the current cell. It brings up the pop-up shown in Figure 60.

If you click on Run Calibre, view feedback, MAX will write out a GDSII file for the current cell, then use the drc_it.calibre script specified by Calibre Shell Script to run Mentor Graphics' Calibre. An example drc_it.calibre shell script is provided in the $MMI_TOOLS/mmi_local.sample/max. If your system administrator followed the install instructions and copied over the mmi_local.sample directory, this script will be in $MMI_TOOLS/../mmi_local/max. This script must be edited to point to your Calibre DRC decks for your technology.

While Calibre is running, messages will print in the MAX command window (the window from which you started MAX).

    Figure 60: Run External DRC 
     

Once Calibre has finished running, MAX will display the Calibre DRC errors on your layout using the annotation layer.

If you instead select View feedback from previous Calibre run, MAX will load the DRC results from a previous Calibre run and bring up the DRC Feedback window. Refer to the DRC Results command for more details on the MAX Calibre interface.

  • Specify Box by:

Flatten Cells 

 Hotkey: None

Flatten the selected cell(s). By default, this command removes the level of hierarchy of the selected cells. This is sometimes called an explode operation. The cell(s) selected must be at the edit cell level of hierarchy. The level of hierarchy associated with the selected cell is removed.

Put flattened layout in a Group: If set, the flattened layout will be placed into a new group sub-cell, which can be moved or edited more easily.

Flatten entire hierarchy: If set, the flatten operation will be run on subcells until entire cell hierarchy is flattened. Otherwise, only the selected cells themselves will be flattened; only one level deep.

Flatten text only: If set, only text (labels) will be flattened, not cells. In other words, text in the sub-cell(s) will be copied into the current cell, according to the options set in the Flatten Setup menu, but the cells themselves will not be affected.

If you select Calibre Setup, the popup form in Figure 69 will appear. This is where you specify the name and location of the script which runs Calibre DRC.

If you click on Run Calibre DRC Now, MAX will write out a GDSII file for the current cell, then use the drc_it.calibre script specified by Calibre Shell Script to run Mentor Graphics' Calibre. An example drc_it.calibre shell script is provided in the $MMI_TOOLS/mmi_local.sample/max. If your system administrator followed the install instructions and copied over the mmi_local.sample directory, this script will be in $MMI_TOOLS/../mmi_local/max. This script must be edited to point to your Calibre DRC decks for your technology.

While Calibre is running, messages will print in the MAX command window (the window from which you started MAX).

    Figure 69: Calibre Setup 
     

Once Calibre has finished running, the feedback (DRC errors) will automatically be loaded into MAX. This will display the Calibre DRC errors on your layout using the annotation layer. Click on Done in the Feedback Setup form. The Calibre DRC errors will be displayed in the DRC Feedback form as shown in Figure 70.

    Figure 70: View Calibre Results 
     

All of the errors are grouped by type of error. If you click on the "+" next to an error type, the list will be expanded to show all of the DRC violations for that type of error. Click on one of the errors will zoom you in on the error. The text of the DRC error (from Calibre) is displayed in the MAX Message Area

You can display DRC errors for the Entire Cell (default) or specify an area. To specify and area in which to view DRC errors (both for MAX and Calibre errors), click on Set Area and then draw out a region with mouse Button-1. This only affects the viewing of DRC errors. Calibre DRC is always run on the entire cell.

DRC Find Next Error 

 Hotkey: Shift-n

Step through each of the DRC errors in MAX. As each DRC error is highlighted, MAX also zooms in on the error. The DRC error explanation is printed in the Command Window and in the MAX Message Area. This has the same functionality as clicking on Next Error in the DRC Feedback window.

DRC Find Next Kind of Error 

 Hotkey: None

Step to next type of error. For example, if you are looking at Metal1 min. spacing errors, this command would skip to the next type of error (for example, Metal2 min. spacing). This command has the same functionality as clicking on Next Kind in the DRC Feedback window.

Note: When viewing errors from the MAX built-in DRC, they are not sorted by error kind, so this command just scans until it finds a new kind of error. This does not mean that all the previous kind of errors have been viewed.

Explain DRC under Box 

 Hotkey: Shift-y

Draw a box over one or multiple DRC error(s) in MAX (white dots). Then select Explain DRC under Box and the DRC information will be printed in the MAX Command Window . If multiple DRC errors are under the box, all of the DRC violations will be listed. This only explains MAX DRC errors, not errors from an external DRC tool such as Calibre.

Clear Selection 

 Hotkey: c

Clear (deselect) all instances or nets that have been selected.

Select under Box 

 Hotkey: Shift-s

Selects paint enclosed by box as well as any cells, gcells, groups or polygons which are either partially or entirely enclosed by the box.

Select under Box (add) 

 Hotkey: None

Add to selection paint enclosed by box as well as any cells, gcells, groups or polygons which are either partially or entirely enclosed by the box.

Select Cell by Name 

 Hotkey: None

Select a cell by name. A pop-up form as shown in Figure 71 will appear. You can then enter the cell name to select from the list of all cells. All instances of the specified cell will be highlighted.

    Figure 71: Select Cell by Name 
     

Select Cell 

 Hotkey: f

Select the instance of a cell or a Gcell that is under the cursor. If there are multiple levels of hierarchy under the cursor, selecting the Select Cell command multiple times will shuffle through the different levels of hierarchy. The Select Cell command starts at the lowest level of hierarchy under the cursor and moves up the hierarchy.

Select Cell (add) 

 Hotkey: Shift-f

Add an additional instance or Gcell to those already selected. This allows you to select multiple instances and/or Gcells and perform operations on the selected instances.

Select Cell (sub) 

 Hotkey: Alt-f

Remove/subtract an instance or Gcell from those already selected. This allows you to select multiple instances and/or Gcells and perform operations on the selected instances.

Select Net 

 Hotkey: s

Select an entire net. If Select Net is invoked from the menu, click with Button-1 on a geometry. The connectivity is traced and highlighted. Using the hotkey, you move the mouse over a geometry and then type the s hotkey. The entire net is highlighted through the hierarchy. All the unique labels associated with the net throughout the expanded hierarchy are listed in the message area. If there are multiple geometries under the mouse, you can toggle through them by typing s again without moving the mouse. You can also use the Probe command to select nets.

Only geometries which are visible are highlighted. To select a net through all levels of hierarchy, internals (see page 66) must be viewed.

Select Net by Name 

 Hotkey: n

Select Net by Name brings up a pop-up form which allows you to specify a net name. The label for the net must be at the current level of hierarchy. The entire net is highlighted through the hierarchy. All the unique labels associated with the net throughout the expanded hierarchy are listed in the message area.

    Figure 72: Select Net by Name 
     

Zoom In: If selected, MAX adjusts/zooms view to center selected net.

Add to Existing Selection: If selected, the net will be added to the selection. Otherwise, all other selections are removed and then the net is selected.

Pattern match name: If selected, MAX will pattern match using the following characters: 

      ?     match any character; 
      *     match zero or more characters; 
      \c    match character c 
      [abc] match any one of the characters in brackets; 
      [a-z] match range of characters; 
     

Select only text, not attached nets: If set, only the text labels themselves are selected, not the nets they are over.

Hint: to search for unattached text, set the text name to "*", and click on Pattern match name and Select only text. A warning will be printed listing all unattached labels in the cell.

Probe 

 Hotkey: Ctrl-Button-1

The Selection Probe displays a list of all the visible objects under the cursor in the current edit cell. Objects that are currently selected are highlighted in the Selection Probe list.

Mouse Button-1 over an item in the Selection Probe window selects or deselects that item in the MAX window.

Mouse Button-2 or Double-Button-1 over a paint rectangle or polygon listed in the Probe Window selects the net attached to that layer in the MAX window.

    Figure 73: Probe Pop-up 
     

Local Menu

This menu contains Tcl-based MAX functions. You can add your own Tcl functions to this menu. An example of this would be running a batch DRC tool on the current cell. The Tcl code for the examples in the Local menu is found in: 

      $MMI_TOOLS/../mmi_local/max.
    Figure 74: Local Menu 
     

extract it 

 Hotkey: None

Extract a netlist for the current cell. This command will flatten the current cell, write out a .ext file and then undo the flatten. To convert the netlist to .sim format, use the ext2sim command.

Help Menu

    Figure 75: Help Menu 
     

Any time the mouse is over a menu option, a basic description of the command is displayed in the Message Area . The Message Area also displays the mouse functions in the current mode. The Help menu provides you with additional help.

About MAX 

 Hotkey: None

Brings up a form with current information about MAX. About MAX will list the version of MAX used, the location of the MAX software, and the current technology.

Current Hot Keys 

 Hotkey: Space
    Figure 76: About MAX Help Form 
     

Hitting the SPACE bar in any mode brings up the list of hot keys for that mode and a description for each hot key. The Save to File button will write out this hotkey information into a text file. The Edit Keymap button brings up the form for editing the MAX hotkeys (see page 45).

Text Commands 

 Hotkey: None

Brings up a list of all text commands. You can use the Apropos field to search for specific functionality. It will search through the text command names and descriptions for the text string typed in. Click on the text command with mouse Button-1 to see a description of the syntax. The syntax of the text commands is also listed in MAX Text Commands Appendix of this manual.
